summaryEn: Founded in Shanghai in 1915 and the only privately-owned mainland bank to reopen in Taiwan, SCSB is unusually well capitalised, controls 57.6% of Hong Kong's Shanghai Commercial Bank, and trades at book value on a 4.1% yield — with earnings that have gone nowhere for four years.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + Wikipedia + statement data; pure-bank framing — the 1915 Shanghai founding, 1965 Taipei resumption, 57.6% Hong Kong stake and 11.3% equity-to-assets credited, but flat EPS 3.33→3.06, a four-year frozen dividend, the 2023Q4 loss quarter and Hong Kong credit exposure stated plainly; FinMind supplies NO margin or ROE data for banks and none were fabricated — the one ROE figure is explicitly labelled derived; the search result conflating Hong Kong's Shanghai Commercial Bank with HSBC was rejected as false; sector Financials → Commercial Banking, foundedYear 1954 → 1915 with both dates disclosed)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
The Shanghai Commercial & Savings Bank (上海商業儲蓄銀行, TWSE: 5876) is the oldest institution in this collection and the only **pure commercial bank** in it — the three other financial companies profiled here are holding groups. It was **founded on 2 June 1915 at No. 9 Ningbo Road, Shanghai**, by Zhuang De-zhi, **Chen Kwang-pu** and others, and became one of the "three southern banks" of Republican-era Chinese finance. After 1949 it established a Taipei head office in **1954**, was approved to resume operations in June 1964, and **formally reopened on 16 June 1965** — the **only privately-owned bank that relocated from mainland China and resumed business in Taiwan**. It **listed only in October 2018**, among the last major Taiwanese banks to do so. *(Taiwan's corporate registry records the local entity's establishment as 1954; the institution itself dates to 1915, and both are stated here.)*

Its structure is unusual. SCSB is the **controlling shareholder of Hong Kong's Shanghai Commercial Bank, holding 57.6%** — a separate institution created when the Hong Kong branch was re-registered locally in 1950, and **not to be confused with HSBC**, which is an entirely different bank. The Hong Kong unit in turn holds **3% of mainland China's Bank of Shanghai**. Beyond Taiwan and Hong Kong, the group operates in **Wuxi, Vietnam (Dong Nai and Bac Ninh), Singapore, Bangkok, Phnom Penh and Jakarta**.

Financially it is conservative to a degree that is itself the story. **Equity of NT$281.0bn against NT$2.489 trillion of assets** is an **equity-to-assets ratio of about 11.3%** — well above the typical Taiwanese bank, meaning SCSB uses materially less leverage than its peers. That caution has a cost: less leverage mechanically produces a lower return on equity, and **earnings have been flat for four years**. Annual EPS ran **NT$3.33 (FY2022) → 3.02 → 2.78 (FY2024) → NT$3.06 (FY2025)**, and the dividend has been **frozen at NT$1.80 since FY2021** — a **58.82% payout** for FY2025. One quarter, **2023Q4, was a small loss (−NT$0.01)**.

At **NT$43.90 the shares trade at 1.02× book and 13.9× earnings, yielding 4.10%**. One data note: **FinMind provides no gross, operating or net margin and no ROE for this company** — those manufacturing metrics do not apply to a bank, and none have been invented for this page. The honest read: **a 110-year-old, unusually well-capitalised bank with a valuable Hong Kong franchise, priced at book value for a 4.1% yield — and going nowhere in earnings.**

The bank was founded on **2 June 1915 at No. 9 Ningbo Road, Shanghai**, by a group including **Zhuang De-zhi** and **Chen Kwang-pu**, who served as general manager. Its name states its original purpose: a **commercial and savings bank**, taking deposits from ordinary savers at a time when Chinese banking was dominated by foreign institutions and traditional native banks. Chen became one of the most influential figures in modern Chinese finance, and the bank grew into one of the **"three southern banks"** alongside the Chekiang Industrial Bank and the National Commercial Bank.

The next four decades scattered it. In **1950**, after the government's relocation to Taiwan, the bank's **Hong Kong branch was re-registered locally as Shanghai Commercial Bank Limited**, becoming a separate legal institution based in Hong Kong. In **1954** a head office was established in Taipei; approval to resume banking came on **29 June 1964**, and the bank **formally reopened on 16 June 1965** — making it the **only privately-owned bank that moved from mainland China and successfully resumed operations in Taiwan**. State-owned banks made the same journey; private ones, with one exception, did not.

What survived the fragmentation was a **controlling relationship**: the Taiwan bank holds **57.6% of the Hong Kong bank**, which in turn holds **3% of Bank of Shanghai** on the mainland — a structure connecting three jurisdictions that emerged from one 1915 institution. *(Hong Kong's Shanghai Commercial Bank is frequently confused with HSBC; they are unrelated institutions.)*

The character formed by that history is caution. SCSB **did not list until October 2018**, decades after its peers, and carries **equity equal to about 11.3% of assets** — a capital buffer well above the Taiwanese norm. A bank that lost its home market once tends to run with more capital than it strictly needs.

- **1915 (2 June)** — Founded at **No. 9 Ningbo Road, Shanghai** by Zhuang De-zhi, **Chen Kwang-pu** and others; Chen serves as general manager.
- **Republican era** — Becomes one of the **"three southern banks"** with the Chekiang Industrial Bank and the National Commercial Bank.
- **1950** — The **Hong Kong branch is re-registered in Hong Kong as Shanghai Commercial Bank Limited**, becoming a separate institution.
- **1954** — Head office established in **Taipei** (the date recorded as the local entity's establishment in Taiwan's corporate registry).
- **1964 (29 June)** — Approved to resume banking operations.
- **1965 (16 June)** — **Formally reopens in Taipei** — the only privately-owned bank to relocate from mainland China and resume operations in Taiwan.
- **2018 (19 Oct)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (5876)**, among the last major Taiwanese banks to go public.
- **2022** — EPS **NT$3.33**; dividend **NT$1.80**.
- **2023** — EPS **NT$3.02**, including a small **loss in Q4 (−NT$0.01)**; dividend **NT$1.80**.
- **2024** — EPS falls to **NT$2.78**; dividend **NT$1.80**.
- **2025** — EPS recovers to **NT$3.06**; dividend **NT$1.80** again — a **58.82% payout**, unchanged for four years.
- **2026Q1** — Net profit of **NT$6.52bn** on revenue of **NT$13.71bn**; assets **NT$2.489 trillion**, equity **NT$281.0bn**.

SCSB's financials describe **a deliberately under-leveraged bank producing stable but stagnant earnings**.

- **A capital buffer well above the norm.** **NT$281.0bn of equity against NT$2.489 trillion of assets** — an **equity-to-assets ratio of about 11.3%**, materially higher than the typical Taiwanese commercial bank. This is the single most distinctive number in the accounts, and it cuts both ways: it is why the bank is safe, and it is why its return on equity is unremarkable. *(A bank's reported "debt ratio" of 88.7% is simply the mirror of this — customer deposits are liabilities, and this is the lowest-leverage profile among the financial companies in this collection.)*
- **Earnings that have not grown.** Annual EPS: **NT$3.33 (FY2022) → 3.02 (FY2023) → 2.78 (FY2024) → NT$3.06 (FY2025)** — four years, no progress. **2023Q4 was a small loss (−NT$0.01)**, the only negative quarter in the record.
- **A dividend frozen for four years.** **NT$1.80 for each of FY2022, FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025**, having risen steadily before that (NT$1.5 in 2014–2016 → 1.8 → 2.0 → **NT$2.05 in 2019** → 1.7 → 1.8). The FY2025 payout ratio was **58.82%**. The dividend is comfortably covered — it simply is not growing.
- **A solid recent quarter.** **2026Q1 net profit of NT$6.52bn** on revenue of **NT$13.71bn**. *(Annualising that against NT$281.0bn of equity implies a return on equity of roughly 9% — a figure derived here for context, not one reported by the company or supplied by the data source.)*
- **Priced as a value stock.** **NT$43.90, 1.02× book, 13.9× earnings, 4.10% yield.** Trading at book value is the market's assessment of a bank that earns steadily and grows slowly.
- **A data caveat worth stating.** The metrics feed provides **no gross margin, operating margin, net margin or ROE** for this company. Those are manufacturing measures with no meaning for a bank, and none have been fabricated to fill the gap. What can be shown — assets, equity, EPS, dividends, price-to-book — is shown.

The financing reality: **a bank that chose safety over leverage and gets a book-value valuation for it**, paying out roughly 59% of steady earnings while the earnings themselves stand still.

**Stance: an unusually well-capitalised 110-year-old bank with a valuable controlling stake in Hong Kong, trading at book value on a 4.1% yield — with four years of flat earnings and a frozen dividend.**

The bull case:

1. **Capital strength that is genuinely differentiated.** **Equity at about 11.3% of assets** — well above the Taiwanese norm. In banking, the institutions that survive credit cycles are the ones that entered them over-capitalised, and SCSB's history explains why it runs this way.
2. **A Hong Kong franchise most investors overlook.** SCSB **controls 57.6% of Hong Kong's Shanghai Commercial Bank**, a long-established local institution, which in turn holds **3% of Bank of Shanghai**. Together with branches in **Wuxi, Vietnam, Singapore, Bangkok, Phnom Penh and Jakarta**, this is a regional footprint disproportionate to the bank's size.
3. **A value price with a covered yield.** **1.02× book, 13.9× earnings, 4.10% yield**, with a **58.82% payout** on earnings that, while flat, are stable. Buying a well-capitalised bank at book value is a conventional value proposition.

The counter-arguments:

- **Earnings have gone nowhere.** **NT$3.33 → 3.02 → 2.78 → NT$3.06** over four years, with a **small loss quarter in 2023Q4**. There is no growth here to re-rate.
- **The dividend has been frozen at NT$1.80 since FY2021.** The yield comes from the price falling to book, not from the payout rising.
- **Hong Kong is a risk as well as an asset.** A 57.6% stake in a Hong Kong bank means exposure to Hong Kong property and credit conditions, which have been weak — and to the territory's broader trajectory.
- **Conservatism caps returns by construction.** Lower leverage means lower ROE. Investors wanting banking returns get a safer, smaller version of them.
- **No margin or ROE data is published by the metrics source**, so profitability must be assessed from EPS, equity and payout rather than from standard ratios.

A **capital-preservation-with-income** thesis: a safe, cheap, slow bank — bought for the balance sheet and the yield, not for growth.

SCSB is a **conventional commercial bank**, and its distinguishing features are structural rather than product-based:

- **The core: deposits and lending.** The bank takes deposits and lends to companies and individuals, earning the spread between what it pays and what it charges, plus fee income. **NT$2.489 trillion of assets** places it among Taiwan's substantial banks without being one of the giants.
- **Not a financial holding company.** This is the important distinction from **CTBC, Fubon and Yuanta**, also in this collection. Those are holding groups combining banking with insurance, securities and asset management. SCSB is a **bank**, so its results reflect lending and deposit-taking rather than a blend of financial businesses — simpler to assess, with fewer offsetting engines when one segment struggles.
- **A controlling stake in a second bank.** SCSB holds **57.6% of Hong Kong's Shanghai Commercial Bank**, a separate institution with its own Hong Kong franchise, which itself holds **3% of Bank of Shanghai**. This gives the group genuine cross-border reach — and ties a meaningful part of its economics to Hong Kong's credit conditions.
- **A regional branch network.** **Wuxi, Vietnam (Dong Nai and Bac Ninh), Singapore, Bangkok, Phnom Penh and Jakarta** — positioned where Taiwanese companies manufacture and trade, which is the natural customer base for a Taiwanese bank abroad.
- **Capital as strategy.** Running **equity at about 11.3% of assets** is a deliberate choice. A bank generates returns by lending its capital several times over; holding more capital per unit of assets means **lower returns in good years and greater survivability in bad ones**.

The levers are **loan growth, net interest margin, credit costs and fee income**. The strength is a **conservatively funded balance sheet with a genuinely differentiated overseas asset**. The vulnerability is the mirror image: **a bank that lends less aggressively earns less**, and four years of flat EPS is what that looks like in practice. Standard manufacturing profitability ratios do not apply, and the data source supplies none.

Taiwanese banking is **overcrowded, over-regulated and structurally low-margin** — and SCSB has responded by not competing on the usual terms.

- **Too many banks chasing the same deposits.** Taiwan has roughly forty domestic banks serving 23 million people, a fragmentation that keeps **net interest margins among the lowest in Asia**. Competition for good corporate borrowers is intense, and price is the usual weapon.
- **Holding companies versus standalone banks.** Most of the sector consolidated into **financial holding companies** — CTBC, Fubon, Cathay, Yuanta — combining banking with insurance and securities to diversify earnings and cross-sell. SCSB **stayed a bank**. That means no insurance float, no brokerage cycle, and no securities trading result to offset a weak lending year — but also none of the volatility those businesses import.
- **Where SCSB is genuinely different.** Two things: **capital**, at roughly **11.3% equity-to-assets** against a sector that runs materially thinner; and **the Hong Kong stake**, a **57.6%** controlling interest in a separate established bank. Neither is available to a domestic peer by choosing to do it — the first is decades of retained earnings, the second is an accident of 1950 history that cannot be recreated.
- **The regional angle.** Branches in **Vietnam, Singapore, Thailand, Cambodia and Indonesia** follow Taiwanese manufacturing across Southeast Asia — the same supply-chain relocation visible throughout this collection, from Johnson Health Tech's Vietnamese plants to Pou Chen's footwear operations.
- **The Hong Kong question.** The 57.6% stake is the bank's most distinctive asset and its most concentrated risk. Hong Kong's property and credit environment has been weak, and the territory's long-run position is genuinely uncertain.

SCSB's position is that of **a conservative survivor in a commoditised industry**. The industry truth is that **in a market where everyone competes on price for the same borrowers, the only durable advantages are capital and access to somewhere else** — and SCSB has both.

**Strengths**
- **Exceptional capitalisation**: equity of **NT$281.0bn** against **NT$2.489 trillion** of assets — about **11.3% equity-to-assets**, well above the Taiwanese norm.
- **57.6% controlling stake in Hong Kong's Shanghai Commercial Bank** (which holds 3% of Bank of Shanghai) — a cross-border asset no domestic peer can replicate.
- **110-year institutional history**; the only privately-owned mainland bank to resume operations in Taiwan; regional branches across Vietnam, Singapore, Thailand, Cambodia and Indonesia.
- **Value pricing with covered income**: **1.02× book, 13.9× earnings, 4.10% yield, 58.82% payout**.

**Weaknesses**
- **Four years of flat earnings**: EPS **3.33 → 3.02 → 2.78 → 3.06**, including a **loss quarter in 2023Q4**.
- **Dividend frozen at NT$1.80 since FY2021**.
- **Low leverage caps ROE by design**; no insurance or securities earnings to diversify.

**Opportunities**
- Southeast Asian branches following Taiwanese manufacturing relocation.
- Capital strength enabling lending expansion or acquisition when peers are constrained.
- Re-rating above book if earnings growth resumes.

**Threats**
- **Hong Kong property and credit weakness** flowing through the 57.6% stake.
- **Taiwan's structurally thin net interest margins** in an overcrowded banking market.
- Interest-rate cycles compressing spreads; competition from larger financial holding groups.

- **Stagnant earnings (the central issue).** **EPS of NT$3.33, 3.02, 2.78 and NT$3.06** across four years is not a growth record, and **2023Q4 produced a small loss (−NT$0.01)**. With the dividend **frozen at NT$1.80 since FY2021**, an investor is buying stability, not compounding — and a bank at book value stays at book value until earnings move.
- **Hong Kong concentration.** The **57.6% stake in Shanghai Commercial Bank** is SCSB's most distinctive asset and its largest single risk. Hong Kong's property and credit conditions have been weak, and deterioration there flows directly into group results. The stake is also illiquid — it cannot be trimmed the way a securities portfolio can.
- **Structural margin pressure.** Taiwan's banking market is fragmented among roughly forty domestic banks, producing some of Asia's thinnest net interest margins. As a standalone bank, SCSB has **no insurance or securities earnings** to offset a weak lending environment.
- **Conservatism limits returns.** Running **equity at about 11.3% of assets** is the reason the bank is safe and the reason its returns are modest. This will not change — it is the institution's character.
- **Credit cycle exposure.** Bank earnings are the residual after credit losses, and losses arrive with a lag. A Taiwanese or regional downturn would show up in provisions well after the economic data does.
- **Limited published metrics.** The data source provides **no ROE, net margin or operating margin** for this company — standard bank-specific disclosures such as the non-performing loan ratio and capital adequacy ratio must be read from company filings, and are not reproduced here because they were not independently verified.

SCSB's outlook is a question of **whether a conservatively run bank can convert its capital strength into earnings growth, or whether it remains a stable income holding priced at book.** The axes to watch:

- **Earnings breaking out of the range.** **FY2022–FY2025 EPS of 3.33, 3.02, 2.78 and 3.06** defines the band. **2026Q1 net profit of NT$6.52bn** was a solid start; a full year materially above NT$3.06 would be the first real change in four years — and the trigger for any move above book value.
- **The dividend.** Held at **NT$1.80 for four years** at a **58.82% payout**. An increase would signal management's confidence that the higher earnings base is durable; another freeze confirms the status quo.
- **Hong Kong.** The **57.6% stake** is the swing factor in both directions. Stabilising Hong Kong property and credit conditions would lift group earnings; further deterioration would do the opposite, and it is the single exposure most worth monitoring.
- **Deployment of capital.** With **equity at about 11.3% of assets**, SCSB has more room than its peers to grow lending or acquire when others are constrained. Whether it uses that room — or continues to hold it — determines whether the capital strength is an asset or merely a cushion.

Bottom line: SCSB is a **110-year-old institution that survived the loss of its home market and rebuilt in Taiwan**, holding **57.6% of a Hong Kong bank**, running **equity at about 11.3% of assets** — materially safer than its peers — and trading at **1.02× book and 13.9× earnings for a 4.10% yield**. It is also a bank whose **earnings have not grown in four years** and whose **dividend has not moved since FY2021**, with meaningful **Hong Kong credit exposure**. Judge it on **EPS breaking above NT$3.06 and any change in the dividend** — a safe, cheap bank that will re-rate only if it starts to grow.
